thread.title: A Familycentric Book (Part 3)

author: Richard and Linda Eyre
title: A Familycentric Book (Part 3)
text:
Author’s Note: Last week the Proctors mentioned that we are partnering with them in exploring the possibility of having a Friday Family-Focused Forum each week here on Meridian. We think it would attract many additional writers, artists and poets who focus on family, marriage, parenting, temple work and family history; and would provide a veritable smorgasbord of ideas, inputs and family experiences for Meridian readers. And we believe many readers would become actively involved by sending in their favorite family moments or ideas.
We’re also partnering with the Proctors on both the creation and the release of our new book which is called FAMILYCENTRIC. It is a coffee-table type book in a beautiful 10-x-10 format filled with full color illustrations and paintings and with family-related poetry interspersed with its essays. The originally projected price for this elegant book was $49.95 but we managed to get it reduced to $29.95 and have arranged an additional 15% discount for Meridian readers when they order the book HERE .
Today’s article is the third in a little “trilogy.” Article 1 was on “A Familycentric World?” ( read here ). Article 2 was on “A Familycentric Church!” ( read here ). Today’s article is on “A Familycentric Book,” and focuses on the artistic side of the book, revealing 8 of the lovely illustrations from Eva Timothy.
Origins A year ago, when we wrote a series of essays for Meridian about a new perspective, a new family-focused “lens” through which to view the Restored Gospel and the Church, we did not know it would turn into a book.
When the high level of interest in the essays caused us to start thinking of expanding them into a book, we knew instantly that it could not be an “ordinary” book — because family cannot be described or discussed with mere words.
We feel our families in our heart as much as we think of them in our brains .
Our own families exist as much in our emotions as they do in our minds. They are an art as well as a science; song as well as a script.
We began to visualize the book not as a textbook closed on a shelf but as an artbook open on a coffee table. The more we thought about it, the more we realized that it needed poetry as much as prose, and art as much as articles.
Luckily, we knew exactly who to turn to.
Our Bulgarian Daughter When our oldest daughter Saren returned from her mission in Bulgaria, she essentially brought one of the converts home with her.
It’s a little more complicated than that, and a little more beautiful. When vivacious 16-year-old Eva Koleva was baptized in Bulgaria, she knew that she wanted to come to Zion, to be part of the Church at its center, to go to school in Utah, and to partake of all the joy she knew was to be found in the Restored Gospel and in the culture and society of the Church.
She essentially asked Sister Eyre if she could come home with her, and Sister Eyre essentially said yes.
So we traveled to Bulgaria to meet this girl and to explore how we could help her and her family. It was 1993, the wall had only recently come down, and Bulgaria and the rest of Eastern Europe still struggled under the remnants of Communism.
Eva’s beloved parents pretty much ran the small Sophia Latter-day Saint branch and district that had survived Communism, and Eva was their only child. We couldn’t imagine taking their daughter so far away, but they tearfully explained that leaving Bulgaria was the only way she (and they) could live their dream.
Eva lived with us for a time and her very presence taught our whole family a level of gratitude and of love for America that we had never known—giving us more than we could ever give her.
We sent her off to Rick’s College, then to the University of Utah, and then on a mission to New York City where she served under Mission President Ronald Rasband.
Her interests turned to art and photography and one Christmas, on a “family date night” we lined her up with the son of two of our best friends and it soon became obvious that she and Adam Timothy were meant for each other. Adam and Eva belonged together as much as their names suggested—and not long after the wedding they were off to Oxford where Adam did an MBA and Eva studied and honed her talents and interests in photography and art.
Book Partners When our vision of the FAMILYCENTRIC book expanded from mental words to include emotional art and poetry, we turned to Eva and Adam. The book grew into something more than we could have hoped for, and Eva, in her lovely and distinctive style, did large, full-page painting to illustrate each of its 20 essays; and Adam designed and laid out the book and added his own brilliant poetry and writing.
But why try to describe it when a picture is worth a thousand words. Let us show you a sample of the “opening art” for eight of the essays or chapters and tell you a bit about why we love each one. And then let us end with a couple of the book’s poems.
Essay 2: The Essential Paradigm Shift I Thought the Family Supported the Church—I Had It Backwards In this essay we try to separate the eternal institution of the Family from the temporary but essential “scaffolding” of the Church, and Eva used the iconic, partially restored Salt Lake Temple to create the connection.
Essay 3: Our Familial Premortal Existence How Our Knowledge of Life Before Life Changes Everything Here we explore the powerful and pivotal nature of our belief in a spiritual life before life—how unique that belief is in the world and how it changes the perspective in which we see everything else. It required an ethereal, imaginative illustration, which Eva produced.
Essay 4: Our Parental God When We Say, “Heavenly Father” We Mean It (Literally) We wanted to explain the ways that the restored understanding of our Heavenly Parents and the knowledge of a Parental (not just Sovereign) God expands and beautifies everything, particularly our prayers. Eva captured the awe and glory of that perspective.
Essay 5: Good Parents Love All Their Children Equally And God Is Not the Exception, but the Example The Eternal and Inclusive context of the Restored Gospel — the everlasting parental love of Heavenly Parents for all of us as their children and each other’s spiritual siblings — is not an easy thing to illustrate, but Eva captured the “connected-ness” in her art.
Essay 8: Turning the Hearts, Lest the World Be Wasted How Society Suffers When the Family Is No longer Its Basic Unit The admonition to “turn the hearts” both from parents to children and from children to parents occurs in each of our Standard Works, and always contains dire warnings about the consequences of not doing so. Eva captured the symbolic longing and links of the Spirit of Elijah.
Essay 10: The Paradigm of Progression The Entity’s Journey toward Completion The Restoration’s view of Eternal Progression is so opposite of the notion of Eternal Rest and our definition of family becomes so much larger and more inclusive when we think Celestially. Eva captures a forever progression in a unique way.
Essay 18: Have We Lost the Family Brand? The Church Was Once Widely Known for Its Family-Focus This essay bemoans the fact that the Church has lost some of the close identification with family that it once had in the public mind, and Eva suggests the return to a more complete family-orientation with this remarkable, artistic summary of President Oaks first address as head of the Church
You Write This One, As Only You Can Write Your Own Family Essay Here, and Plant It in Your Heart The final essay of the book is one that the reader is asked to write, and poses questions to help us each to solidify our own personal beliefs and views about God’s Eternal Family and our own Earthly Families. How to draw down that inspiration and record it is the suggestion of Eva’s illustration.
We hope the book’s familycentric lens will help each of us bring into sharper focus both our own families and our place in our Heavenly Parents’ family, and we are so grateful for Adam and Eva’s partnership in that vision.
Let’s conclude with a couple of poems from the book: What Makes Sense to Me
By Richard Eyre
Life,
Is made up of causes and effects,
Doings and endings,
Actions and results,
Journeys and Destinations,
Choices and consequences,
Plans and goals,
Means and Ends.
We each struggle to determine our desired ends,
And search for the means to reach them.
And that wrestle is the essence of existence,
The fabric and factual fabrication of what we do,
Every day.
It creates and defines purpose,
And meaning,
And it can be a clarifying framework
for understanding the deepest things,
Like God
And His wisdom.
What is God’s end, and God’s means?
What is His goal, and His plan?
Would they be too complex for mere mortal minds?
Or would they lie beyond complexity where all is
Condensed into clarity?
End: The Immortality and Eternal Life of Man.
Means: Mortal experience and Infinite Atonement
Expansion: His children journeying, expanding, likening, returning
And thus partaking of the Full Joy that He wants us to have;
The physical falling facilitating the spiritual flowering,
Its lost trajectory boomeranged by
The justice-robbing mercy of Christ’s Atonement.
Forging Family
By Adam Timothy
A place of pure belonging
Soul songs, echoes
memories of home ago
and return’s anticipation
Hearth and hearts knit
fire’s side stories
this feeling of together
forging family
A sense so sure secure
room left for learning
flying and then falling
into waiting arms
A piercing sense of purpose
protect provide
nurture nourish
grow gather glorify
The parental push and pull
concentric circling
of light lived
lessons learned
Fierce faith followed
friction…sparks then
generations of steady breath
on tender embers
Yearnings of eternity
turning towards
expanding outwards
receiving freely giving
Resonance beyond reason
offered whole
made more
one forever
family
